messages.text: I’ll use `/kk:brainstorm` to work through whether a cross-run cache is worth pursuing, keeping manual invocation and local processing as settled decisions.

A cross-run cache could save most of that 20-second wait when a report is requested again while its inputs are unchanged. Its value depends on how often that happens; “public data only” remains an assumption to verify before deciding to persist results.

Manual invocation and local processing stay settled.

How commonly do users rerun the same report with unchanged inputs—several times in a working session, across days, or rarely?

That correction rules out cross-run caching of report data. It depended on persistence being acceptable; encryption or a short expiry cannot satisfy the rule that no report data survives process exit.

Manual invocation and local-only processing remain settled.

The useful alternatives are reducing computation time and, if one process repeats work, reusing results during that process’s lifetime. We don’t yet know whether either would materially reduce the 20-second wait.

The next step is to investigate where those 20 seconds go. Cache formats, eviction policies, and cross-run invalidation can be dropped from this decision.

You’ve decided to drop cross-run caching and investigate computation time before considering optimization.

- Reports contain confidential customer data, and no report data may persist after exit—even encrypted. That rules out caching report results across runs.
- Manual invocation and local-only processing remain settled.
- Each invocation produces one report, so repeated report requests within a process don’t provide a reason to cache.
- The current 20-second wait is tolerable. The investigation may or may not reveal a worthwhile improvement; no optimization is committed.

Next: identify where computation time goes, then assess any potential improvement against its cost. Implementation details can wait.
